title: The 6 Best Affirmation Apps for iPhone and Android in 2026
description: The best affirmation apps for iPhone and Android in 2026, compared by what each lets you do with the words, where it puts them during your day, and what it costs after the trial: Believe, I am, Gratitude, Innertune, ThinkUp, Anicca and Mantra, verified against App Store listings read in November 2026.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

All five of the main affirmation apps in this comparison have been on phones at the same time, in the roundups that rank them and in the stores that sell them. What makes them blur together is easy to see: the wallpapers change, the fonts change, and underneath sits the same set of sentences about worthiness and abundance, poured into a new gradient every year, wrapped in a subscription, and shipped. For the longer store-checked comparison by delivery method, see our [full guide to the best affirmation apps](https://aniccaai.com/blog/best-affirmation-apps-2026-11-05), for yesterday's comparison by how each app works, see [Best Affirmation Apps 2026: ThinkUp, I Am, Innertune](https://aniccaai.com/blog/best-affirmation-apps-2026-11-13), and for iPhone only, see our [guide to the best affirmation apps for iPhone](https://aniccaai.com/blog/best-affirmation-apps-for-iphone-2026-11-12).

The differences that matter are not in the words. They are in what the app lets you do with them, where it puts them during your day, and what it charges once the trial ends. That is what this comparison measures. Anicca, our own app, is added at the end of the list and in its own section, scored by the same four questions, and it is not ranked first.

*Disclosure: Anicca, the app added sixth here, is made by the team behind this site. Believe, the app ranked first here, is made by the team behind the comparison this page follows. No app paid to be here.*

## How we judged these

Four questions decided the order:

1. **Can you make it yours?** An affirmation you scroll past is a quote. One you wrote, or recorded in your own voice, or said to your own reflection, is a different object entirely.

2. **Does it reach you during a real day?** Not a spa morning. A Tuesday. Widgets, lock screens, a watch face, notifications that arrive while you are stuck somewhere.

3. **What does it cost after the trial?** All of the apps below are free to download. None of them stay free in their full form.

4. **Is it still open in month two?** This is the only question that really matters, and it is the one most roundups skip.

Ranked against those four, the order below does not match the download charts.

## The six at a glance

| App | Best for | Standout | Get it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Believe | The most complete practice | Affirmation Mirror, voice recording, widgets, watch | iOS · Android |
| I am | Sheer scale | 738,672 US ratings, huge library | iOS · Android |
| Gratitude | Journaling and vision boards | Vision board, guided challenges | iOS · Android |
| Innertune | Passive listening | Audio playlists that run while you sleep | iOS · Android |
| ThinkUp | Voice recording, if that is all you want | Record and replay over music | iOS · Android |
| Anicca | A short card on a difficult day, with no streaks | Choose your topics, get short cards by notification | iPhone |

## 1. Believe: Daily Affirmations

Believe ranks first in the comparison this page follows because it is the only app there that does not force a trade. Most of these apps are built around one good idea. Believe carries the good ideas from all of them and adds one nobody else in that five has.

### What sets it apart

The **Affirmation Mirror** puts your own face behind the words while you say them. No other app on the original list has anything like it, and it changes the exercise completely. Reading "I am enough" on a gradient is a different act from saying it while looking yourself in the eyes.

The **voice recorder** lets you record affirmations in your own voice and replay them, which is the entire premise ThinkUp is built on. **Timed practice sessions** with ambient music and medal milestones give the repetition somewhere to go, so you can sit with one line for four minutes instead of consuming forty in four. A **gratitude journal** covers the ground Gratitude specialises in. **More than 10,000 affirmations** across dozens of categories answers the library question that makes I am popular.

Then there is reach: home screen widgets, lock screen text, and an Apple Watch face, so the affirmation finds you at a stop light or in an elevator instead of waiting for you to remember it. Add 300+ themes, dark and light modes, and full English and Spanish, and the practical answer to "which one should I install" gets short.

> The best affirmation app is the one that makes you stop for four seconds and actually mean it. Everything else is decoration.

### Where it gives ground

Believe launched in June 2021, which makes it younger than I am (2014), ThinkUp (2014) and Gratitude (2018). That shows up in one number: 367 ratings on the US App Store against I am's hundreds of thousands, as reported in the comparison this page follows. The average there is higher, 4.9 against 4.8, but the crowd is smaller, and for some people the crowd is the point. It also has no vision board, so if a visual collage is central to how you practice, Gratitude does that and Believe does not.

## 2. I am: Best for sheer scale

I am is the category. On the App Store since May 2014, 4.8 stars from 738,672 US ratings when we checked in November 2026, and the app most people mean when they say "affirmation app." The library is enormous, the typography is lovely, the widgets and lock screen delivery are excellent, and the notification cadence is tuned by a team that has studied this for over a decade. Premium on the US listing is $60 a year, $15 a month or $150 lifetime; see the store page for current prices in your country.

### Where it wins

Nothing else here has that much social proof, and social proof is a real reason to trust an app with a daily habit. If you want zero decisions and a beautiful sentence appearing on your lock screen with no input from you, I am does that better than anyone.

### Where it falls short

The relationship stays one-directional. You receive affirmations, you rarely make them, and after a few months many people report reading them the way they read a headline. There is no mirror, no timed session structure, and no journal in the comparison this page follows. Its listed in-app purchases also run higher than the rest of this group, so check the annual price rather than the monthly one before you commit.

## 3. Gratitude: Best for journaling and vision boards

If affirmations at a mirror have never done much for you, the format may be the problem rather than the practice, and Gratitude is the strongest alternative here. It wraps affirmations inside a journal, a vision board, and guided challenges, so the affirmation arrives attached to something you actually wrote about your own week.

### Where it wins

The vision board is genuine, and it is the one feature in this roundup that Believe does not answer. Journaling depth is real too: photo entries, voice journals, and prompts better than most dedicated journaling apps. The comparison this page follows reports 4.9 stars across nearly 45,000 ratings since 2018.

### Where it falls short

Affirmations are one module inside a larger self-care product rather than the point of it, so a focused daily affirmation habit means navigating past a lot of other features. The app will not push you toward one specific practice on its own, so the habit has to come from you.

## 4. Innertune: Best for passive listening

Innertune is the newest here, released November 2022, and it goes audio-first. You build playlists of spoken affirmations layered over music and let them run while you work, drive, or sleep. Its store listing describes about 77,000 affirmations across 550+ playlists, 19 voices plus an ASMR option, 100+ binaural beat tracks, a night mode for sleep, daily reminders, personalised 21-day plans, streaks, and recording in your own voice. At 4.8 stars across about 12,000 US ratings when we checked, plenty of people find that it fits them. Premium is $29.99 a year on the US listing.

### Where it wins

Passive playback genuinely suits anyone already listening to podcasts or ambient audio for hours a day, and meeting an existing habit beats fighting one. Believe has ambient music inside its sessions, but it does not do standalone sleep playlists in the same way, so this is a real distinction.

### Where it falls short

Passive is the design and passive is the failure mode. Audio playing near you is not the same as deciding to mean something, and if it fades into background noise you get nothing while noticing nothing. It also has no Apple Watch app in the comparison this page follows, which rules out the wrist entirely.

## 5. ThinkUp: The original voice-recording app

ThinkUp arrived in December 2014 and built its reputation on one idea: record affirmations yourself, in your own voice, and play them back over music. Hearing your own voice tell you something is a materially different experience from reading it in someone else's font, and ThinkUp got there first. Its US listing is the cleanest on price in this group: $7.99 a month, $39.99 a year, or $99.99 for lifetime access, at 4.7 stars from about 7,500 ratings when we checked.

### Where it falls short

That idea is not its own anymore. Voice recording now ships in other apps on this list as well, so there is much less reason to pick ThinkUp specifically. The interface shows its age next to Gratitude or I am, the curated library of 300+ affirmations is smaller, and it holds about 7,500 ratings against competitors with tens or hundreds of thousands. It ranks fifth in the original comparison because everything it does well, something else on this list also does, usually alongside more.

## 6. Anicca: A short card, with no recording to make

[Anicca](https://aniccaai.com/affirmation-app) is our app, and by the four questions above it is deliberately narrower than the five above. You choose what you are struggling with, enable notifications, and receive short cards to read. There is no voice recorder, no mirror, no journal, no vision board and no audio library, and we do not pretend otherwise. It requires iOS 16.6 or later, it is iPhone only, and it has no streaks.

### Where it wins, by the same questions

On question two, reach during a real day, its whole design is the notification card: a short line arrives, you read it, and the practice is over in seconds, with no session to start. On question four, month two, there is no streak to break and no library to keep up with, so a missed day costs nothing. Its US listing showed 5.0 stars from 1 rating and its Japanese listing 4.5 stars from 48 ratings when we checked in November 2026, and Premium is $59.99 a year on the US listing. Those are small numbers next to I am's 738,672 US ratings, and we print them as they are.

### Where it falls short

If you want to hear your own voice, sit in a timed session, keep a journal, build a vision board or fall asleep to a playlist, every app above does something Anicca does not. It is also iPhone only, where the five above are on Android as well. Pick it only if a short, kind card on a difficult day is the practice you will actually keep.

## Also worth knowing: Mantra

Mantra missed the original list on a technicality. Around since February 2017, 4.8 stars across about 34,000 ratings when we checked, 1,000+ "I am" affirmations in 30+ categories, own-voice recording, and widgets among the prettiest on iOS. It is not in the five because it is iPhone only in the comparison this page follows, and roughly half of the people reading a cross-platform roundup are on Android.

## Why delivery decides it

This is where most people underestimate the decision. Search the App Store for "affirmation" and the top suggestions after the category name itself are *affirmation widget*, *affirmation lock screen* and *affirmation reminder*, in the comparison this page follows. People are not really shopping for sentences. They are shopping for delivery.

The research backs the instinct. A University College London study on habit formation found that automaticity builds through repeating a behaviour in a consistent context, and took a median of 66 days to plateau. Two things follow from that. The cue matters as much as the action, and month two is precisely when the habit is still being built rather than finished.

The affirmations that stick are rarely the ones you sit down to read. They are the ones that show up at a stop light, in an elevator, while something else is running. An affirmation you have to remember to open is one you will stop opening around week three. One already sitting on your lock screen, or arriving as a short notification card, when you check the time has no activation cost at all.

Only two apps in the original five cover all three surfaces properly, in that comparison: **Believe** offers home screen widgets, lock screen affirmations and an Apple Watch face, and **I am** matches it with widgets, lock screen delivery and a watch app. Innertune has no watch app at all. Anicca covers one surface, the notification card, and covers only that. Before you commit to any affirmation app, check the widget, lock screen and notification support specifically, because that is the feature that decides whether you are still using it in month two.

## What's free, and what isn't

All of these apps are free to download, and all of them put their best features behind a subscription. That is the business and it is fine. What is less fine is how hard several of them make it to see the real number before you commit.

On a free tier you can generally expect a limited daily affirmation or two, a small slice of the categories, and basic reminders. The things people actually stay for — the full library, the mirror, voice recording, unlimited categories, premium themes and most widget customisation — sit behind the paywall in every app here.

Listed in-app purchase ranges vary widely, which tells you how much variation hides behind identical-looking "Start free trial" buttons. Before subscribing to any of them, find the annual price rather than the monthly one, check whether a lifetime option exists, and set a calendar reminder for the day before the trial ends. Doing that once saves more than most of these apps cost. For Anicca, the annual price is the one we print above: Premium $59.99 a year on the US listing.

## How to choose

Pick by the way you want to practice, not by the download count.

- **You want the most capable app and the fewest compromises:** Believe.
- **Social proof and the biggest possible library matter most:** I am.
- **A vision board and deep journaling are central to how you practice:** Gratitude.
- **You want it playing in the background while you sleep or work:** Innertune.
- **You only care about recording your own voice:** ThinkUp, though other apps here do this too.
- **You want a short card by notification, chosen by what is on your mind, with no streaks and nothing to record:** Anicca.

Then delete the others. Several affirmation apps on one phone is a way of practicing none of them.

## The app is not the practice

Most of these apps feel interchangeable because most of them stopped at the same idea: show a nice sentence on a nice background. The ones worth keeping are the ones that give the sentence somewhere to land, through your own voice, your own reflection, your own words, or a card that arrives on a screen you were already looking at.

That is a smaller promise than the App Store descriptions make, and it is the one that holds up. So pick one and give it long enough for the cue to start doing the work for you. Sixty-six days, if the research is right, though you will probably notice something shift well before then.

The app is only scaffolding. What you are building is the habit of talking to yourself like someone worth believing. You can read Anicca's own page at [aniccaai.com/affirmation-app](https://aniccaai.com/affirmation-app).
